source.title: Stochastic Gradient and Langevin Processes
source.authors: Xiang Cheng; Dong Yin; P. Bartlett; Michael I. Jordan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices and experiment details, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The experiments vary SGD batch size and report that test accuracy tracks noise covariance, with no significant correlation to batch size or step size once covariance is considered. This qualifies the claim that batch size itself predicts a generalization penalty.
record.gate_note: The study reports CIFAR-10 test-accuracy results for standard SGD and large-noise SGD. Training accuracy is described as almost 100% in most experiments, but no separate training-error results are reported. The covariance-versus-test-accuracy values are plotted; the text gives qualitative conclusions, not per-run numbers. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study varies batch size and learning rate at a fixed 2000-epoch budget and measures held-out accuracy. It also tests whether injecting noise lets batches of 256 or 512 match the accuracy of batch 128. These results bear directly on V5's batch penalty and recipe-adaptation clauses.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find that covariance strongly predicts final test accuracy and that matched-covariance noise constructions yield similar accuracy despite different higher moments. They hypothesize that the constant-noise limiting SDE has similar test error; the experiments do not prove a general theory of generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use standard SGD and a custom large-noise SGD variant to study noise covariance, rather than directly reproducing the batch-size comparisons in the claim version. The paper also develops convergence theory for Langevin-like processes.
record.method_sensitivity: Test accuracy varies with noise covariance; when conditioned on covariance, it is not significantly correlated with step size or minibatch size. Large-noise SGD is reported to have similar accuracy to vanilla SGD at matched covariance.

fits_no_version.finding: Across ordinary and injected-noise SGD, matched covariance predicts similar test accuracy despite different higher noise moments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested CNN and VGG19 runs on CIFAR-10, the covariance scalar strongly predicts final test accuracy across different noise constructions.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The empirical study is limited to two architectures on CIFAR-10. Results are largely plotted, without numerical run-level values or uncertainty estimates. Training accuracy is described as almost 100% in most experiments, but no separate training-error measurements are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible reported results found. Theoretical convergence bounds concern Langevin-like process convergence rather than the claim's generalization versions; cited results from other studies are excluded.

missing.what: Separate accuracy improvement over the original same-batch, same-learning-rate baseline after increasing noise covariance eightfold. R3 and R4 currently record only agreement with matched-covariance references, omitting this adaptation outcome.
missing.locator: Section 6.3.2, Figure 3 and its caption; separate results for CNN and VGG19 at batches 256 and 512

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V5. Its covariance-conditioned result does not challenge a claim that already permits recipe adaptations. Accuracy similarities and trends are qualitative in the supplied text, without run-level numerical estimates or reported uncertainty; near-perfect training accuracy is stated for most experiments.

rows.stage_stated: trained 2000 epochs; constant step size; no batch normalization or dropout
rows.operation_detail: Compared final test accuracy across standard SGD runs with different step sizes and minibatch sizes, against noise covariance.
rows.measure: Final test accuracy versus noise covariance (for (δ, b)-SGD, δ/b).
rows.value: Higher noise covariance leads to better final test accuracy; conditioned on noise covariance, test accuracy is not significantly correlated with step size or minibatch size.
rows.note: Figure values are not transcribed as numbers. The text describes the overall relationship across runs for this architecture.
rows.check: The positive accuracy relationship with δ/b supports a larger-batch penalty at fixed learning rate; Section 6 explicitly states that increasing batch size worsens generalization consistently with these experiments. Conditioning on δ/b changes the recipe and does not negate that result. Replace the unspecified baseline with smaller-batch runs at the same learning rate and epoch budget. The paper calls δ/b noise covariance as shorthand for the scalar multiplying H(w).

rows.baseline: Vanilla SGD run with the corresponding noise covariance; exact accuracy not stated.
rows.value: Large-noise SGD produces similar test accuracy to vanilla SGD runs with the same noise variance; plotted points fall close to the linear trend.
rows.note: The text reports similarity and proximity to the trend but gives no per-run accuracy values.
rows.check: Split Figures 3 and 4 into separate comparisons. For Figure 4, the adapted batch-256/512 runs match ordinary batch-128 SGD at the same learning rate, so the remaining batch penalty is absent. The noise-estimation batch size is 128; the main update batch remains 256 or 512. Figure 3 instead increases covariance eightfold relative to its baseline and improves accuracy; its matched-covariance reference uses an eightfold larger learning rate.

relationships.condition: Ordinary SGD on CIFAR-10 with CNN and VGG19, fixed learning rate, 2000 epochs, batches 32–512
relationships.reason: R1 and R2 report better accuracy at higher δ/b; Section 6 explicitly identifies worse generalization with larger batches as consistent with these experiments.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest smaller batches achieved better accuracy at the fixed learning rate. These results have not been verified.

relationships.condition: Noise-adapted SGD on CIFAR-10 with CNN and VGG19, main batches 256 or 512 versus ordinary batch 128, 2000 epochs
relationships.reason: R3 and R4, corrected to isolate Figure 4, report similar accuracy after matching smaller-batch noise covariance, supporting V5's recipe-adaptation clause.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest that larger batches preserved accuracy when their gradient noise had the same variation and correlations as smaller-batch gradient noise. These results have not been verified.

reader_labels.reason: Test accuracy is reported to track noise covariance, while step size and minibatch size are not significantly correlated with it once covariance is conditioned on; matched-covariance large-noise runs have similar accuracy to vanilla SGD (R1–R4). The study does not directly establish a large-batch penalty at fixed recipe.
